title: Pauri 12, sound: mannai
hook: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 11, the last listening stanza. Your line was the blind find the way. Did listening show you a way when looking didn't? Today, a new word takes over. Day one hundred eighty-two.

It's the end of a week, so look back at the road. Pauri 7 told us fame is not it. Then came suniai, by listening, and four stanzas of it: the power of listening, the lowly singing praise, santokh, enough, and yesterday the blind finding the way. That's a whole week of ears. But you know the difference between hearing advice and taking it. Your friend says, get some sleep, and you hear it, and you stay up anyway. Hearing is the first step. Something else has to happen for the words to move in. Japji knows this. Today it changes its word.
screen: `A WEEK OF LISTENING.` → `HEARING ADVICE, TAKING IT.` → `A NEW WORD.`

segments.voice: The new word is mannai. Say it with the n held a moment: MUN-nai. It comes from the Punjabi verb mannanaa, and that verb is wide. It means to accept, to agree, to obey, to believe, to trust, to take something to heart. When a Punjabi mother tells a child, gall mann lai, she means take my word, go along with it. In Japji, mannai means by trusting, by taking the Word to heart. For the next four stanzas, pauris 12 to 15, every line begins with it, the way the last four began with suniai. Listen to the first line of Pauri 12 in the original: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae. Mannai kee, of the one who trusts. Gat, the state, the condition someone is in. Kahee na jaae, cannot be told. The state of the one who trusts cannot be put into words. Hear the rhythm: mannai kee gat, three quick beats, then kahee na jaae, slowing down, as if the sentence itself runs out of breath. Tomorrow we'll open what it means. Today is for the sound. And notice the order Guru Nanak chose. First suniai, listening. Then mannai, trusting. Sikh teachers often describe the path this way: you hear the Word, then you take it in, and later in Japji the stanzas move toward living it. Hearing and trusting sound almost alike in English, too: a word goes in the ear, then it goes home.
screen: `MANNAI — BY TRUSTING.` · `ACCEPT, OBEY, TAKE TO HEART.` · `MANNAI KEE GAT KAHEE NA JAAE.` · `FIRST LISTEN, THEN TRUST.` · then, large: `MANNAI.`

segments.voice: Say mannai slowly, five times. Let each one take a full breath out: MUN-nai. Hold the n, then let the ending open. Between each, rest in the quiet for a few breaths. If it helps, think of one thing you've heard and haven't yet taken to heart, and let the word sit beside it. Then just sit, breathing, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mannai. By trusting, by taking the Word to heart. It begins every line of pauris 12 to 15, after four stanzas of listening.
Your line: mannai, trusting. Today, take one piece of good advice you've already heard, and actually follow it, once. Day one hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; pauris 12 to 15 each begin with mannai, and many who recite them hear the move from suniai, listening, to mannai, trusting, as steps on one path.

original.note: Gurmukhi: mannai, by trusting or accepting; from mannanaa, to accept, obey, believe.

trapdoor: what you thought: mannai means believe.
what it means: by trusting, by accepting the Word and taking it to heart.
what a scholar hears: from mannanaa, which covers agreeing, obeying and believing; it opens every line of pauris 12 to 15, as suniai opened 8 to 11.
